title: Robert Hall’s 1983 proposal to index IOR
contentHtml:
Today’s post is brought to you by my sponsor, Mechanize. They’re hiring junior software engineers at $300K/year base salary. Apply now!

[I did most of this post on Nobel Prize winner Robert Hall a month ago and finally got around to finishing it today.]

One of my favorite papers is a 1983 Robert Hall publication in the Journal of Monetary Economics. Here is a key passage discussing the intuition of Hall’s proposal to stabilize the price level by paying interest on reserves in a way that is indexed to the price level:

The case where reserve certificates [RCs] are perfect substitutes for other forms of government or private debt is particularly interesting. As a general matter, the price level will be indeterminate in this case. However, I will show that a particular form of indexing eliminates the indeterminacy.

The central problem with a fiduciary monetary system is the following: In the absence of inefficient regulatory intervention, the demand for reserve certificates is unpredictable and possibly unstable. But the purchasing power of the certificate is determined precisely by that demand. How can the price level be kept on target in an economy with a fiduciary monetary system with unregulated financial institutions? The answer pursued in this paper is to make the demand for reserve certificates highly elastic with respect to the price level. Small changes in the price level are then enough to offset large shifts in the demand for reserve certificates.

Linking the earnings of reserve certificates to the price level is the technique explored in this paper for improving the performance of a fiduciary monetary system. The basic idea is easiest to understand in the case where the reserve certificate is perfectly substitutable for other components of the government debt; that is, nobody wants to hold certificates because of their unique monetary role, but only because they are interest-bearing instruments with the same return as Treasury bills [TBs]. Then the public’s demand for reserve certificates will have a knife-edge character — demand will be zero if RCs pay less than TBs, indeterminate if they pay the same, and very high if RCs pay more than TBs.

Let the policy for paying interest on RCs be the following: an RC earns the TB interest rate plus an extra 1 percent per year for each percent by which the price level exceeds 100. Then the only possible price level is 100. If prices exceed 100, RCs pay more than TBs, and the public will want to move all of its wealth from TBs to RCs. Changes in interest rates cannot clear the market, for the interest on RCs is linked to the market TB rate. On the other hand, if prices fall short of 100, RCs earn less than TBs, and nobody will want RCs at all. Again, the market cannot clear at this price level. If prices are exactly 100, the public willingly holds whatever combination of RCs and TBs that the government has decided to put on the market. Therefore, the only possible price level is 100, and that is the competitive equilibrium price level.

Although it may not be obvious at first glance, I believe that this proposal is quite similar to my various proposals to use either price level or nominal GDP futures targeting. I asked ChatGPT to interpret Hall’s proposal. My two questions will be in italics, and I won’t indent ChatGPT’s responses.

Question 1: Robert Hall has a 1983 Journal of Monetary Economics paper that proposes a monetary policy that utilizes market forces to stabilize the price level. How does this proposed policy work?

ChatGPT said:

Robert E. Hall’s 1983 paper, Optimal Fiduciary Monetary Systems, proposes a way to stabilize the price level by using the market demand for bank reserves as an automatic stabilizer, rather than relying entirely on a central bank to adjust the quantity of money. The paper appeared in the Journal of Monetary Economics, volume 12, issue 1, pages 33–50.

The central insight is that the central bank can influence the purchasing power of money by changing the return banks earn on reserves in response to the price level. This makes banks’ own decisions about how many reserves to hold part of the mechanism that stabilizes prices.

How the policy works

Hall’s proposal has two key ingredients: interest-bearing government money and returns indexed to the price level.

1. If the price level rises above target

The monetary system makes holding the monetary instrument less attractive in real purchasing-power terms. This encourages portfolio adjustments that reduce the demand for money and put downward pressure on prices.

2. If the price level falls below target

The mechanism works in reverse: holding the monetary instrument becomes more attractive, encouraging greater demand for it and putting upward pressure on prices.

3. Market responses stabilize prices

Banks and other market participants adjust their holdings in response to the instrument’s return. These decentralized portfolio decisions help counteract disturbances to money demand without requiring the central bank to fine-tune the quantity of money continually.

The important distinction is that the proposal combines market-rate interest with price-level indexation. It is not simply a rule to raise interest rates whenever inflation rises; it changes the terms of the monetary instrument itself.

Why this is different from conventional monetary policy

Under conventional policy, a central bank typically changes interest rates or its balance sheet to influence spending and inflation. Hall’s approach instead seeks to build a self-correcting feedback mechanism into the monetary system.

The goal is a homeostatic monetary system: one in which the demand for the monetary instrument responds to economic disturbances in ways that help keep the price level stable. The mechanism is intended to work even when money demand shifts for reasons unrelated to monetary policy.

For further reading, Hall and Ricardo Reis revisit this idea in their later paper, Achieving Price Stability by Manipulating the Central Bank’s Payment on Reserves (2016). It develops the price-level-indexed reserve-payment mechanism more explicitly.

Question 2: I’m confused. A reduced demand for money tends to reduce the value of money, which means a higher price level, not a lower price level.

You’re absolutely right. A reduction in the demand for money, holding the supply of money and other factors constant, puts upward pressure on the price level. My previous explanation had the causal direction backward.

The basic relationship is:

where M is the money supply, V is velocity, P is the price level, and Y is real output. If people want to hold less money, velocity tends to rise; with M and Y unchanged, P rises.

So my claim that making money less attractive would reduce the price level was incorrect.

The actual mechanism in Hall’s proposal

Hall’s idea is subtler than the mechanism I described. In Optimal Fiduciary Monetary Systems, he proposes a monetary instrument whose return pays the market interest rate and is also indexed to the price level. The objective is to make the price level stable through financial-market arbitrage.

The key is to distinguish the demand for money from the terms of the monetary instrument:

  • A change in money demand, by itself, can indeed move the price level in the direction you describe.

  • Hall’s proposal changes the instrument’s payoff rules so that arbitrage between it and other financial assets helps pin down the price level, even when money demand changes.

In other words, the stabilizing force is not that reduced money demand lowers prices. It is that the monetary instrument’s indexed payoff structure makes its market value adjust in a way that counteracts price-level disturbances.

Your objection exposes a real error in my earlier explanation: I described the direction of the money-demand channel incorrectly. Thank you for catching it.

*********************

OK, this is me again. Hall’s proposal is obviously not easy to understand. If ChatGPT is struggling with the proposal, then I guess I’m not yet completely obsolete (but for how much longer?)

For some strange reason Hall’s 1983 paper was widely ignored. Indeed, even Hall himself seemed to ignore this paper in future research. For instance, in 2016 he coauthored a paper with Ricardo Reis that seems remarkably similar to the 1983 JME paper, without citing that earlier paper. Even more oddly, Hall seemed to go out of his way to cover up the existence of the 1983 proposal. This is from the 2016 paper with Reis:

Hall (1997) appears to be the first statement of the idea that the price level can be controlled by a security whose purchasing power is designed to be constant, although he noted that Irving Fisher proposed that the monetary unit could be a quantity of gold that is adjusted continuously.

Wasn’t Hall (1983) the “first statement”? Was there some flaw in the 1983 paper that explains why it doesn’t seem to be cited in Hall’s future work? I’m not sure. Below the break I’ll discuss why I view Hall’s 1983 proposal (and later work with Reis) as being similar to ideas such as NGDP futures targeting.
